source_text:
Quid ergo mirum, si iam inminente templorum et simulacrorum euersione, quam prophetae dei summi tanto ante praedixerant, Serapis daemon alicui cultorum suorum hoc de proximo prodidit, ut suam quasi diuinitatem recedens uel fugiens commendaret?
Fugantur enim isti uel etiam iussis superioribus conligati abstrahuntur et alienantur a locis suis, ut de rebus, quibus dominabantur quibusque colebantur, fiat uoluntas dei, qui hoc tanto ante per omnes gentes futurum esse praedixit et, ut per suos fideles fieret, imperauit. cur autem hoc non sineretur daemon praedicere. cum sibi iam praenosceret inminere, cum haec praedictio et prophetis adtestaretur, a quibus sunt ista conscripta, et prudentibus daretur intellegi, quam uigilanter esset daemonum cauenda fallacia cultusque fugiendus? qui cum ante per tam longum tempus in templis suis haec futura tacuissent, quae per prophetas praedicta ignorare non possent, posteaquam adpropinquare coeperunt, uoluerunt ea quasi praedicere, ne ignari uictique putarentur. cum igitur tam longe ante praedictum esset atque conscriptum, ut alia interim taceam, illud, quod Sophonias propheta dicit: praeualebit dominus aduersus eos et exterminabit omnes deos gentium terrae, et adorabunt eum unusquisque de loco suo, omnes insulae gentium, aut non credebant ista sibi euentura, qui in templis gentium colebantur, et haec ideo per suos uates ac fanaticos frequentare noluerunt — sicut eorum poeta Iunonem inducit non omni modo credentem, quae de Turni morte Iuppiter dixerat: Iuno autem ab istis potestas aeria praedicatur, quae apud Virgilium sic loquitur: nunc manet insontem grauis exitus, aut ego ueri uana feror. quod ut o potius formidine falsa ludar et in Melius tua, qui potes, orsa reflectas! — aut ergo ista sibi, quae per prophetas praedicta nouerant, posse accidere daemones, hoc est potestates aeriae, dubitabant et propterea praedicationem eorum celebrare noluerunt — et hinc intellegendum est quales sint — aut, cum ea uentura certissime scirent, ideo per sua templa tacuerunt, ne iam tunc inciperent ab hominibus intellegentibus deseri atque contemni, quod de templorum et simulacrorum suorum futura euersione eis prophetis adtestarentur, qui eos coli prohibebant. nunc uero, posteaquam tempus aduenit, quo conplerentur uaticinia prophetarum dei unius, qui istos falsos deos dicit et. ne colantur, uehementissime praecipit, cur non hoc etiam ipsi completum praedicere sinerentur, unde clarius adpareret eos haec antea uel minime credidisse uel suis cultoribus enuntiare timuisse, in fine autem, tamquam nihil amplius habentes quod agerent, etiam ibi uoluisse suam ostendere diuinationem, ubi iam produntur diu simulasse diuinitatem?
nunc manet insontem grauis exitus, aut ego ueri
uana feror. quod ut o potius formidine falsa
ludar et in Melius tua, qui potes, orsa reflectas! —
thought_title: Demons' late prediction of temple destruction
orientation: Augustine is answering why a demon of Serapis predicted the destruction of the temples and idols just before it happened, when God's prophets had foretold it long before.
pass_a_gloss: What therefore is strange, if now when the overthrow of temples and idols was imminent, which the prophets of the highest God had predicted so long before, the demon Serapis disclosed this to one of his worshipers from near at hand, so that by departing or fleeing he might commend his own quasi-divinity? For these beings are put to flight, or even, bound by higher commands, are dragged away and removed from their places, so that concerning the things over which they ruled and by which they were worshiped, the will of God may be done, who predicted so long before that this would happen through all the nations and commanded that it be done through his faithful ones. But why should this not be allowed to be predicted by the demon, when he already knew beforehand that it was imminent for himself, when this prediction both would bear witness to the prophets, by whom these things were written down, and would be given to the wise to understand how vigilantly the deceit of demons must be guarded against and their worship must be fled? These beings, when for so long a time before in their temples they had been silent about these future things, which they could not be ignorant had been predicted through the prophets, after these things began to draw near, they wished to predict them, as it were, so that they would not be thought ignorant and conquered. Therefore, when it had been predicted and written down so long before—to pass over other things in the meantime—that which the prophet Zephaniah says: the Lord will prevail against them and will exterminate all the gods of the nations of the earth, and they will worship him, each one from his own place, all the islands of the nations, either they did not believe that these things would happen to them, who were worshiped in the temples of the nations, and for this reason they did not wish to repeat these things through their own seers and fanatics—just as their poet introduces Juno not entirely believing what Jupiter had said about the death of Turnus: but Juno is proclaimed by these people as an airy power, who in Virgil speaks thus: now a heavy end awaits the innocent man, or I am carried along, empty of truth. Would that I may rather be played with by false fear, and that you, who can, may turn back your undertakings for the better!—either therefore the demons, that is the airy powers, doubted that these things which they knew had been predicted through the prophets could happen to them, and for this reason they did not wish to celebrate their prediction—and from this it must be understood what sort they are—or, when they knew most certainly that these things would come, for this reason they were silent through their temples, so that they would not then begin to be deserted and despised by understanding men, because they would bear witness to the prophets about the future overthrow of their temples and idols, who forbade that they be worshiped. But now, after the time arrived in which the prophecies of the prophets of the one God were fulfilled, who says that these are false gods and most vehemently commands that they not be worshiped, why should they not also be allowed to predict this fulfillment, from which it would appear more clearly that they had either least believed these things before or had feared to announce them to their worshipers, but at the end, as if having nothing more that they could do, they wished to show their divination even there, where they are now exposed as having long pretended divinity?

choices.why: Keeps the dismissive force of 'quasi'—Augustine denies that the demon has real divinity.
Matches the brief's 'airy body' language and keeps the plural 'powers' as a title for demons.

choices.english: I am carried along, empty of truth
choices.why: Renders the Virgil quotation literally: 'uana' as 'empty of truth' preserves the sense of being deceived.
rejected: I am borne along in vain
I am carried away by empty things

choices.english: so that they would not be thought ignorant and conquered
choices.why: Keeps both adjectives in the predicate and the passive force of 'putarentur'.
rejected: lest they be thought ignorant and defeated
so as not to seem ignorant or beaten

choices.why: The perfect infinitive 'simulasse' with 'diu' captures the completed pretense over a long time.
rejected: that they had long counterfeited divinity

bible_refs.note: praeualebit dominus aduersus eos et exterminabit omnes deos gentium terrae, et adorabunt eum unusquisque de loco suo, omnes insulae gentium

pass_b_english: What wonder is it, then, that when the overthrow of the temples and idols was already at hand—the overthrow that the prophets of the most high God had predicted so long before—the demon Serapis disclosed it to one of his worshipers just before it happened, so as to commend his own quasi-divinity by departing or fleeing, as it were?

For these demons are put to flight, or even bound by higher commands and dragged away and removed from their places, so that concerning the things over which they ruled and for which they were worshiped, the will of God may be done. God predicted this long before throughout all the nations, and commanded that it be accomplished through his faithful ones.

But why should the demon not be allowed to predict this, since he already foresaw that it was imminent? For this prediction would both bear witness to the prophets by whom these things were written down, and give the wise an opportunity to understand how watchfully one must beware the deceit of demons and flee their worship. They had kept silent in their temples for so long a time about these future events, which they could not have been ignorant were predicted by the prophets. But after these events began to draw near, they wanted to predict them, as it were, so that they would not be thought ignorant and conquered.

Since it had been predicted and written down so long before—to pass over other things for now—what the prophet Zephaniah says: “The Lord will prevail against them and will exterminate all the gods of the nations of the earth, and all the islands of the nations will worship him, each from his own place” (Zephaniah 3:9)—either those who were worshiped in the temples of the nations did not believe these things would happen to them, and for that reason did not want to spread them through their own seers and fanatics—as their poet introduces Juno not entirely believing what Jupiter had said about the death of Turnus: “Now a heavy end awaits the innocent man, or I am deceived about the truth. Would that I might rather be mocked by false fear, and that you, who are able, might turn your undertakings to the better!”—or the demons, that is, the airy powers, doubted that these things predicted by the prophets could happen to them, and therefore did not want to celebrate their prediction—and from this one may understand what sort of beings they are—or, since they knew with complete certainty that these things would come, they kept silent in their temples so that they would not begin even then to be abandoned and despised by people of understanding, because the prophets who forbade worshiping them bore witness to the future overthrow of their temples and idols.

But now, after the time has come when the prophecies of the prophets of the one God are being fulfilled—the God who calls these false gods and most vehemently commands that they not be worshiped—why should they not also be allowed to predict the fulfillment itself? From this it would appear more clearly that they had either not believed these things before, or had feared to announce them to their worshipers, and that at the end, as if having nothing more to do, they wanted to display their divination even there, where they are now exposed as having long pretended divinity.

problems.why: Latin means 'throughout all the nations' (spatially), not 'by means of all nations' or 'through all nations' as agents.

edits.old: God predicted this long before through all the nations, and commanded that it be accomplished through his faithful ones.
edits.new: God predicted this long before throughout all the nations, and commanded that it be accomplished through his faithful ones.

fixed: Changed 'through all the nations' to 'throughout all the nations' because the Latin 'per omnes gentes' is spatial, not instrumental.

problems.quote: or I am carried along, empty of truth
problems.why: 'Uana feror' means 'I am borne along by empty/vain things' or 'I am deceived by idle fancies,' not 'empty of truth.' The ablative 'ueri' is partitive/genitive of respect: 'vain in respect of truth' = 'deceived about the truth.'
problems.fix: or I am deceived about the truth

problems.quote: and each one from his own place will worship him, all the islands of the nations
problems.source_quote: et adorabunt eum unusquisque de loco suo, omnes insulae gentium
problems.why: English mistranslates: 'unusquisque de loco suo' = 'each from his place'; subject of 'adorabunt' is 'omnes insulae gentium', not 'each one'.
problems.fix: and all the islands of the nations will worship him, each from his own place
problems.ruling: Source 'unusquisque de loco suo' is subject of 'adorabunt'; 'omnes insulae gentium' is vocative/address, not subject. English inverts subjects, misrepresenting syntax.

problems.source_quote: praeualebit dominus aduersus eos et exterminabit omnes deos gentium terrae, et adorabunt eum unusquisque de loco suo, omnes insulae gentium
problems.why: Citation is Zephaniah 3:9 LXX/Vulgate, not 2:11. The verse numbering differs significantly.
problems.ruling: Source quotes Zephaniah; '2:11' is wrong numbering. Vulgate Zeph 2:11 matches but LXX differs; citation needs verification.

edits.old: or I am carried along, empty of truth
edits.new: or I am deceived about the truth

edits.old: and each one from his own place will worship him, all the islands of the nations
edits.new: and all the islands of the nations will worship him, each from his own place

fixed: Changed 'or I am carried along, empty of truth' to 'or I am deceived about the truth' because 'uana feror' means being borne along by empty things or deceived, not 'empty of truth.'

Changed 'and each one from his own place will worship him, all the islands of the nations' to 'and all the islands of the nations will worship him, each from his own place' because 'omnes insulae gentium' is the subject of 'adorabunt', and 'unusquisque de loco suo' is distributive.
Changed 'Zephaniah 2:11' to 'Zephaniah 3:9' because the quoted text corresponds to Zephaniah 3:9 in the Septuagint/Vulgate numbering.

last_rejected.quote: the God who calls these false gods
last_rejected.why: dicit here means 'denounces' or 'declares to be', not 'calls'; God denounces them as false gods.
last_rejected.fix: the God who denounces these as false gods
last_rejected.ruling: 'Calls' is within normal range for dicit; 'calls false gods' clearly conveys denunciation in context.

last_rejected.quote: the demon Serapis disclosed it to one of his worshipers just before it happened
last_rejected.source_quote: Serapis daemon alicui cultorum suorum hoc de proximo prodidit
last_rejected.why: "de proximo" means "from nearby/near at hand" (i.e., the demon was nearby/fleeing), not "just before it happened."
last_rejected.fix: the demon Serapis disclosed it from nearby to one of his worshipers, as if departing or fleeing
last_rejected.ruling: "de proximo" can mean "recently/just now"; rendering as "just before it happened" is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: so as to commend his own quasi-divinity by departing or fleeing, as it were
last_rejected.source_quote: ut suam quasi diuinitatem recedens uel fugiens commendaret
last_rejected.why: The participle "recedens uel fugiens" modifies Serapis, not the manner of commending; he commends his divinity while fleeing.
last_rejected.fix: so as to commend his own quasi-divinity as he withdrew or fled
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly has Serapis departing/fleeing; participles modify him, not manner of commending.

last_rejected.quote: For these demons are put to flight
last_rejected.why: "Fugantur" is passive (they are driven away/put to flight), but the English loses the passive force and agency of higher powers.
last_rejected.ruling: "put to flight" preserves passive force; agency specified next clause. Minor preference only.

last_rejected.why: "iussis superioribus" means "by the commands of higher powers/beings," not abstract "higher commands."
last_rejected.fix: bound by the commands of higher powers
last_rejected.ruling: "higher commands" adequately renders "iussis superioribus"; no meaning lost or reader misled.

last_rejected.quote: concerning the things over which they ruled and for which they were worshiped, the will of God may be done
last_rejected.source_quote: ut de rebus, quibus dominabantur quibusque colebantur, fiat uoluntas dei
last_rejected.why: The English makes "the will of God" the subject of a new clause, but Latin "fiat voluntas dei" is purpose/result of their removal.
last_rejected.fix: so that God's will might be done regarding the things over which they ruled and by which they were worshiped
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly expresses purpose clause "fiat voluntas dei"; no structural or semantic error.

last_rejected.quote: God predicted this long before throughout all the nations, and commanded that it be accomplished through his faithful ones
last_rejected.source_quote: qui hoc tanto ante per omnes gentes futurum esse praedixit et, ut per suos fideles fieret, imperauit
last_rejected.why: The relative "qui" refers back to "dei" (God's will), not introducing a new sentence about God; "per omnes gentes" modifies prediction, not accomplishment.
last_rejected.fix: who predicted long before that this would happen throughout all nations, and commanded that it be accomplished through his faithful ones
last_rejected.ruling: "qui" refers to God; new sentence acceptable. "per omnes gentes" with prediction is clear enough.

last_rejected.quote: why should the demon not be allowed to predict this
last_rejected.source_quote: cur autem hoc non sineretur daemon praedicere
last_rejected.why: Missing "autem" (but/however); more importantly, "praedicere" here means "to proclaim/publish" (make public), not predict.
last_rejected.fix: But why should the demon not be allowed to proclaim this
last_rejected.ruling: "autem" is minor; "praedicere" can mean predict/foretell. No major error.

last_rejected.quote: For this prediction would both bear witness to the prophets
last_rejected.source_quote: cum haec praedictio et prophetis adtestaretur
last_rejected.why: "cum" is causal/ concessive here ("since/because"), not "for"; the prediction attests to the prophets' truth, not bears witness to them as persons.
last_rejected.fix: since this prediction would attest to the prophets
last_rejected.ruling: "For" renders causal "cum" adequately; "bear witness to prophets" conveys attesting to their truth.

last_rejected.quote: give the wise an opportunity to understand how watchfully one must beware the deceit of demons and flee their worship
last_rejected.source_quote: et prudentibus daretur intellegi, quam uigilanter esset daemonum cauenda fallacia cultusque fugiendus
last_rejected.why: "prudentibus daretur intellegi" is impersonal ("it would be given to the prudent to understand"), not "give the wise an opportunity"; "cultusque fugiendus" = "and their cult to be fled," not "flee their worship."
last_rejected.fix: and it would be given to the prudent to understand how vigilantly the deceit of demons must be guarded against and their cult fled
last_rejected.ruling: "Opportunity to understand" paraphrases impersonal construction adequately; "flee their worship" = cultus fugiendus.

last_rejected.quote: they wanted to predict them, as it were
last_rejected.why: "quasi" modifies the whole act (they quasi-predicted, i.e., made a show of predicting), not "as it were" attached to "wanted."
last_rejected.fix: they wanted, as it were, to predict them
last_rejected.ruling: "As it were" correctly attaches to quasi-predicting; no reader misled.

last_rejected.quote: so that they would not be thought ignorant and conquered
last_rejected.why: "ignari" = ignorant (of what was coming), but "uictique" = "and defeated/vanquished," not "conquered" in sense of being overcome in knowledge.
last_rejected.fix: so that they would not be thought ignorant and defeated
last_rejected.ruling: "Conquered" is valid synonym for "uicti"; no meaning changed.

last_rejected.quote: did not want to spread them through their own seers and fanatics
last_rejected.source_quote: haec ideo per suos uates ac fanaticos frequentare noluerunt
last_rejected.why: "frequentare" means "to repeat, practice, celebrate, spread abroad" (make frequent), but "fanaticos" here means "possessed persons/frenzied devotees" (those through whom demons spoke), not "fanatics" in modern sense.
last_rejected.fix: did not want to have them repeated through their own seers and possessed devotees
last_rejected.ruling: "Fanatics" is archaic for frenzied devotees; within normal range, not modern sense.
